issues.issue: The clause deems listed liability policies to include a "Broad Exclusion Provision" whose text is never set out in the instrument, so the content of what is deemed included cannot be determined. The enumerated coverage list also has no catch-all, leaving unlisted hospital coverages outside the deeming.

Payment "without diminution because of the insolvency of the ceding insurer" pulls against Article IV's definition of loss as amounts "actually paid by the REINSURED," though Article IV expressly carves out insolvency, and against the offset right in c038.

The exception "except as provided by Section 4118 of the Insurance Law of New York" imports New York statute into a treaty between a Kansas reinsurer and an Ohio cedent that contains no governing-law clause. Whether that provision has any operation here is left unaddressed.

Notice "within a reasonable time after such claim is filed in the insolvency proceeding" sets no measurable period and no consequence for failure. It sits alongside the separate and differently worded "prompt notice" duty in Article IX (c033).

"[A] proportionate share of the benefit which may accrue to the ceding insurer solely as the result of the defense undertaken" gives no method for measuring either the benefit or the proportion. "Solely" further narrows it in a way that is hard to apply.

"[A] majority in interest" of reinsurers is undefined — whether measured by limit, premium or number — and the apportionment is directed to be made "in accordance with the terms of this reinsurance agreement," which contains no apportionment formula for multi-reinsurer expense.

"CRNA's — each full-time equivalent x 5-10" states a range rather than a rate and gives no rule for choosing a point within it, so the premium base is indeterminate. The remaining multipliers are fixed, which sharpens the contrast.

Territory 1 is defined as "the remainder of the states of Ohio, Maryland, Kentucky, Illinois, Nebraska, Wyoming and Arizona not listed in Territories 2," so an account in any other state falls into no territory and carries no multiplier. The enumeration is closed with no residual category.

"[N]et profit accruing to the REINSURED under this agreement" is an odd formulation, since Article VII defines net profit as the excess of credits over charges in the reinsurer's accounting, not something accruing to the cedent. The base of the 40% is therefore contestable.

The proviso confining the commission to "the first $1,000,000 of reinsured limits as respects each policy" cannot be worked through Article VII's Accounting Schedule (c025–c026), which computes profit treaty-wide from written premium, paid and unpaid losses with no per-policy or per-layer allocation.

The revised exclusion (a) drops "by the insured" and now excludes "loss arising out of the operation of a teaching hospital" without defining teaching hospital, even though (b) defines "total beds" with care. The reach of the exclusion to a hospital with any residency programme is open.

The revised list drops Cuyahoga County, Ohio from the excluded territories while Rating Schedule-A and -B place Cleveland in the highest-rated Territory 3; the two treatments of the same risk are consistent only on a rating rationale that is nowhere stated.

"$25,000,000 each occurrence, $25,000,000 annual aggregate" does not say whether the aggregate applies per ceded policy or across all cessions in a year, and "each occurrence" is left undefined. That is the standard aggregation question in an excess treaty.

This amendment deletes Article III outright, yet Amendment No. 1 applies only "as respects policies becoming effective on or after July 1, 1995," so it is unclear whether the original $10,000,000 limit (c009) survives for 1994–mid-1995 cessions or was wiped out.

The trigger is a self-insured Hospital Professional Liability limit "of $1,000,000/$3,000,000," but the retained layer is then described as $1,000,000 each occurrence/$1,000,000 annual aggregate, so the aggregate figures do not match. Which aggregate the 90%/10% split attaches to is left open.

"In all other respects not inconsistent herewith" is the only priority rule between the original treaty and the amendment, and it neither identifies what counts as inconsistent nor says which text prevails. It is the hinge on which the surviving terms of a five-times-amended instrument turn.

As in the original Rating Schedule, "CRNA's — each full-time equivalent x 5-10" gives a range with no rule for selecting the applicable factor, leaving the occupied bed equivalent count indeterminate for that item.

Territory 1 lists states "not listed in Territories 2 or 3," but Michigan appears only in Territory 2 as "All areas except Wayne and Oakland County," so Michigan risks outside those counties and any risk in an unlisted state have no assigned multiplier. The enumeration leaves gaps rather than a residual class.

Amendment No. 2 adds Iowa and South Dakota to Territory 1 of Rating Schedule-A, but Amendment No. 4 deletes Rating Schedule-A in favour of Rating Schedule-B (c086), whose Territory 1 omits Iowa and South Dakota — silently undoing this amendment.
"In all other respects not inconsistent herewith" supplies no test for inconsistency and no rule of priority among the successive amendments. It is the only reconciliation clause in the instrument.

This deletes and replaces the first paragraph of Article I with one that applies the agreement only to "policies becoming effective on or after October 1, 1996," which read literally leaves the 1994–1996 cessions with no operative application clause even though Article XI's run-off and the Stipulation of Termination assume they remain covered.

The added Schedule entry states the same coverage twice — "Nursing Homes and Outpatient Facilities Professional Liability" and then again "Outpatient Facility Professional Liability" — with identical limits, an evident duplication that leaves the intended entries unclear.

Exclusion (k) excludes "outpatient facilities with employed physicians who provide patient care" but the carve-out speaks of "medical directors and other administrative positions," a category that by definition does not provide patient care — so the proviso either does no work or contradicts the exclusion. "[F]ire resistive" and the unlabelled "surgicenters, emergicenters, hospices or laboratories" item add further indeterminacy.

"[L]imits of $25,000,000 each occurrence and $25,000,000 annual aggregate" does not state whether the aggregate is per ceded policy, per insured risk, or treaty-wide per year, and "occurrence" is defined only for claims-made forms by c083. That leaves the outer boundary of the reinsurer's exposure open.

The amendment deletes Article III "as amended by Amendment No. 1" while itself applying only to policies becoming effective on or after October 1, 1996, leaving it unclear which retention article governs cessions made between July 1, 1995 and October 1, 1996.

The self-insured trigger refers to an underlying limit "of $1,000,000/$3,000,000" but the retained layer is described as $1,000,000 each occurrence/$1,000,000 annual aggregate, so the two aggregates conflict within the same sentence. The drop-down point for the 90%/10% split is correspondingly uncertain.

The $10,000,000 sub-limit for Nursing Home and Outpatient Facility business sits inside a grant of $25,000,000 (c080) without saying whether a loss touching both hospital and nursing home exposures erodes one limit or both.

"[E]ach claim shall be deemed an occurrence hereunder" leaves "claim" undefined, so it is unresolved whether multiple claimants or multiple suits arising from one medical incident are one occurrence or many — the point on which the per-occurrence limit and retention turn. A single sentence of deeming language does the aggregation work for the whole treaty.

The deeming cannot be squared with Article I's Schedule of Underlying Limits, which measures Hospital Professional Liability by "each medical incident" and General Liability by "each occurrence," nor with Article III's occurrence and annual aggregate caps, which assume a single occurrence definition.

"In all other respects not inconsistent herewith" is the only rule reconciling Amendment No. 4 with the original treaty and Amendments Nos. 1–3, and it does not say which text prevails where they differ (for example on Article I's scope and Article III's limits).
"CRNA's — each full-time equivalent x 5-10" again states a range with no selection rule, so this element of the occupied bed equivalent calculation is indeterminate.

Territory 1 lists states "not listed in Territories 2 or 3," yet Washington and Michigan appear in none of the three territories in this schedule, so accounts there have no multiplier at all. The list is closed with no residual category.

"[I]ncidental owned automobile exposure" is undefined and the triggers — "Any Owned Ambulances involved in emergency runs" or "More than 10 owned automobiles" — do not say whether the extra rates then apply to the whole fleet or only the excess. The premium consequence turns on that reading.

"The conversion period will be three years" does not say from what date it runs or how it interacts with the five-year claims-made credit table immediately above it. The bare sentence supplies no starting point.

An extended reporting endorsement "at no additional cost" sits against Article I (c006), under which such an endorsement is part of the policy period but "a separate Limit of liability may apply," and against Article VI's requirement that premium be developed from the Rating Schedule — free cover with a possible fresh limit.

The premium is a percentage of "OHIC's Manual GL and Professional Liability Premium (before application of experience and schedule rating)," a figure generated by one party under a manual not attached to or defined by the agreement. The reinsurance premium therefore depends on an external, uncontrolled document.

The First Million may be modified by schedule credit or debit "at the REINSURED'S discretion but not to exceed 25% for a credit" — the credit is capped but the debit is not, and the discretion is otherwise unbounded and unstandardised. Nothing states what factors may support the modification.

The layer descriptions and the corresponding percentages are set out in two detached columns, so which factor attaches to which million is not determinable from the text as written. The lead-in also speaks of "the next $9,000,000" while nine separate layer factors follow.

"Each million in limits is subject to a minimum premium of $1,000,000" sets a minimum premium equal to the entire limit purchased, which cannot be what was meant when the hospital minimums in the same schedule run from $20,000 downward. That is a plain mis-writing that changes the meaning of the provision.

"[T]he excess factors from the preceding paragraph" has no antecedent: the preceding paragraph gives per-$1,000-receipts imaging rates, and the Excess Factors appear in a later section of the same schedule. The cross-reference cannot be followed as written.

The schedule credit or debit is "at OHIC's discretion but not to exceed 25% for a credit," capping only the credit and leaving the debit and the criteria for either wholly at large. The same asymmetry appears in c093.

"[T]he first million is subject to a minimum premium of $1,500,000 and each additional million thereafter ... $1,000,000" sets minimum premiums exceeding the limits purchased, which is an evident mis-writing when the hospital minimum premium tables in the same schedule are in the thousands. The figures cannot be applied as written.

The stipulation terminates the treaty "with respect to loss under policies issued on or after January 1, 1998," a cut-off keyed to policy issuance that does not track Article XI's termination machinery (c039) or its run-off and extended-reporting continuation provisions (c040, c041). Whether policies issued before that date, and their extended reporting endorsements, remain reinsured and for how long is left to be worked out between the two texts.
